description: R²C Analog Solutions, presenta un dispositivo (Lab-S) capas de calcular ecuaciones diferenciales de segundo orden para representar fenómenos fisicos. Para el challenge Flame in Freefall, diseñamos un simulador web que recopila datos experimentales, cuenta con una IA para responder preguntas y un apartado donde se puede calcular la evolución temporal de la temperatura y la tasa de liberación de calor, a su vez se esta adaptando Lab-S para representar fenómenos utiles para la NASA.
summary: PYRA + Lab-S is a fire-safety decision tool for crewed space missions that pairs a digital dashboard with a physical analog computer. NASA’s microgravity combustion experiments are public but scattered and hard to compare. PYRA gathers 14 reference experiments (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, MIST), ranks fire risk for the ISS, Moon, Mars and Earth, recommends protocols, and simulates a compartment’s temperature rise from oxygen, airflow and gravity using a second-order model solved with RK4. An AI assistant answers natural-language questions, with a local fallback knowledge base when offline. The Signals Laboratory (Lab-S) is a modular analog platform built with operational amplifiers (Biquad Tow-Thomas filter) that solves the same second-order equation continuously in real time, already validated with an RLC circuit. Because both share one equation, the hardware cross-checks PYRA’s numerical results and shows on an oscilloscope how overshoot, settling time and threshold crossings change with damping. Time and amplitude scaling map PYRA’s scenarios onto the Lab-S range, and a test plan compares measured traces with predictions. The same hardware emulates other dynamic systems by changing coefficients.
details:
Flame in Freefall asks for a way to make decades of NASA microgravity fire data usable for safety decisions. Crews on the ISS and future Moon or Mars habitats cannot easily flee a fire, and the data on how flames behave without gravity, or in partial gravity, is spread across many experiments with different fuels, facilities and variables. Our solution has two parts that check each other.

PYRA is a single-page web application with four tabs. The Overview tab selects an environment and shows its risk index, required detection time, recommended protocol and a curve of flame spread against airflow. The NASA Experiments tab is a searchable catalog of 14 reference scenarios, filterable by campaign and risk, that can be loaded directly into the simulator. The Simulator lets users adjust oxygen, airflow, gravity and damping, and calculates temperature, heat release rate, settling time and whether the compartment is nominal, igniting or in thermal runaway. The Assistant answers questions in natural language through an AI model and falls back to a local knowledge base when there is no connection. The thermal model is a second-order differential equation, solved numerically with the fourth-order Runge–Kutta method.

The Lab-S is a modular analog platform built at IPET N°66 in Argentina. It uses a Biquad Tow-Thomas active filter made of three operational amplifiers, a power supply, signal generators with a Schmitt trigger, an equation module, and an operations module with an adder and multiplier. Its component values are adjustable: resistance sets the damping, inductance sets the natural frequency, and capacitance is fixed. Its enclosure was designed in FreeCAD for 3D printing. Because the circuit integrates continuously, it has no time-step error, and it has already reproduced the expected transient of an underdamped RLC circuit on an oscilloscope.

The two parts are linked by the fact that PYRA’s thermal equation has the same form as the Lab-S filter equation. A time-scale factor of 2 × 10⁴ makes PYRA’s 60-second scenarios run in about 3 ms on screen, and an amplitude scale converts the output voltage back into degrees. Using this mapping we calculated the component settings for four scenarios, including a lunar habitat with enriched oxygen, which PYRA rates as the most critical environment. The numerical and continuous solutions agree to within 0.001 °C.

The benefits are practical. Mission planners and safety engineers can compare hundreds of experiments in one place, and crews and students can see, on a real oscilloscope, how overshoot and settling time depend on damping, which is hard to convey from a chart. The hardware is low-cost, uses common components and works without a network or software, so it can serve as an independent verifier in schools and training laboratories. Since the Lab-S solves a general second-order equation, the same board can emulate an RLC circuit or a mass-spring-damper system by changing only the coefficients.

The intended impact is safer human spaceflight and better fire-safety training. The project is not yet a certified tool: PYRA’s coefficients are phenomenological and must be calibrated against NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics records, the partial-gravity scenarios are extrapolations, and the Lab-S predictions have not yet been measured with PYRA’s parameters. Next steps are calibration, measuring the predicted traces, and adding an analog-to-digital converter so PYRA can read the Lab-S output and compute the error automatically.

What made the project creative is the pairing of a software dashboard with an analog computer. Instead of only computing a fire’s evolution, the team makes that evolution visible in real time, turning an abstract differential equation into a waveform. The approach also inverts a common assumption: a software model is checked by a second, physical solver built from the same mathematics.

In designing the solution, the team considered crew safety and the specific atmospheres of planned habitats, the gap between 1 g Earth tests and microgravity, and the limits of current data. They also weighed accessibility: the hardware and the dashboard must work for schools without special equipment or constant connectivity. Finally, the team paid attention to reproducibility, documenting every constant, scaling factor and assumption so that others can verify or extend the work
